pages.title: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms
pages.content:
Greedy algorithms is a type of algorithm, where you try to take the best option at every step, and it ends up giving the best solution in the long run as well.

Let's imagine that we are in a rectangular maze where we are starting from the bottom-left corner and we know that the exit is at the top-right. So one approach that we might try, is that at every step, we try to go up, and if that is not possible, we try to go right. 

This is a 'greedy' choice, where we are choosing what seems to be locally the best choice, but actually, the path which goes up might end in a dead end, and we actually need to take a longer path which starts out by going left! But when we talk about greedy algorithms, we are talking about problems where we know (rather we have proven), that such things don't happen. And we are sure that taking the locally best option does indeed lead to the correct optimal solution.

So, as you might have guessed, implementing a greedy solution is often easy. The hard part lies in figuring out when and where you can apply a greedy solution. And that typically involves us trying to prove that a greedy solution works, which can be hard some times.

So let us dive into the world of greedy algorithms!

pages.title: Max Boy-Girl Pairs
pages.content:
You have a row of students, each either a girl ('x') or a boy ('y'). Students standing next to each other are friends. You need to form as many dance pairs as possible, where each pair consists of one boy and one girl who are friends. Each student can only be in one pair.

**Example 1:**\
Input: xy\
Students: Girl ('x') and Boy ('y') standing next to each other.\
Possible pairs: (Girl, Boy)\
Output: 1 (only one pair can be formed)


**Example 2:**\
Input: xyxxy\
Students: Girl ('x'), Boy ('y'), Girl ('x'), Girl ('x'), Boy ('y')\
Possible pairs: (Girl 1, Boy 2) and (Girl 4, Boy 5)\
Or (Boy 2, Girl 3) and (Girl 4, Boy 5)\
Output: 2 (two pairs can be formed)

**Example 3:**\
Input: yy\
Students: Boy ('y') and Boy ('y')\
Possible pairs: None (no girls to pair with)\
Output: 0


The goal is to find the maximum number of such pairs for any given string of students.**

checkpoint.question: In the Chopstick Pairing problem with difference threshold D = 10, the smallest stick is 20 and the second smallest is 40. What can be deduced?
options: Stick 20 cannot pair with stick 40 or any larger stick (40 - 20 = 20 > 10), so stick 20 can never be paired
Stick 20 and 40 form a valid pair
All remaining sticks are invalid
We must restart with an unsorted array
checkpoint.explanation: Since the sticks are sorted, any stick after 40 has length >= 40. The difference with stick 20 will be at least 40 - 20 = 20 > D. Thus, stick 20 cannot pair with any stick and must be discarded.

pages.title: Is It Greedy
pages.content:
### Recognizing Greedy Choice Monotonicity

A problem exhibits the **greedy choice property** if a globally optimal solution can be reached by making a series of locally optimal choices without backtracking.

Key traits of greedy problems:
1. **Optimal Substructure:** Optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
2. **Greedy Choice Property:** Making the best choice right now never invalidates future optimal choices.

A greedy algorithm commits to the best-looking local choice and needs a correctness argument showing that the choice can be safely extended to an optimal solution.

**Recognition rule**

pages.teachingGoal: Explain the idea in plain language and identify when it should be considered.

pages.title: Strategy - Optimal Subset Selection
pages.content:
Since we cannot take all the elements, lets take the alternate elements.

That is take all the even-indexed numbers together in one subset and all the odd-indexed numbers together in another subset. The resultant answer would be the greater one of both.

Also, we will optimise this strategy further by always rejecting negative numbers.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Strategy - Optimal Subset Selection and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

options: Apply the correct algorithmic idea and handle the specified edge cases

Use unrelated data structures
Assume the largest possible answer is always correct
checkpoint.explanation: The lesson on Strategy - Optimal Subset Selection is mastered by applying the intended algorithm correctly and respecting the problem constraints.

pages.title: Greedy Strategy
pages.content:
Since that didn't work out, let's try to take the largest element of the integers first, then the second largest, and so on.

If at any point we cannot take an element (if either of its neighbours is already taken), we will skip that element.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Greedy Strategy and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Another Strategy
pages.content:
To overcome the last issue, this time we would consider the largest number, then the second largest number, and only take the number if it is greater than the sum of its neighbours; otherwise, we will instead pick neighbours.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

pages.content:

pages.title: Guided Implementation

- Translate the invariant into variables.

- Check initialization.
- Check loop/condition boundaries.

referenceSolution.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){int n;cin>>n;vector<int>a(n);for(auto&x:a)cin>>x;int l=0,i=0,r=n-1;while(i<=r){if(a[i]==0)swap(a[l++],a[i++]);else if(a[i]==2)swap(a[i],a[r--]);else i++;}for(int k=0;k<n;k++){if(k)cout<<' ';cout<<a[k];}cout<<'\n';}

topics.title: Intervals
topics.description: Merge, insert, schedule, and select intervals with clear boundary invariants.

pages.title: Prerequisite Check
pages.content:
Before solving Intervals, confirm the learner can identify the input shape, the operation being requested, and the expected complexity target.

- State the input and output in your own words.
- Identify the simplest correct baseline approach.
- Name the constraint that can make the baseline too slow.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
Intervals is easier to master when the rule is reduced to one repeatable mental model. Start with the data state, the operation, and the condition that permits each update.

- Identify the state that must be maintained.
- Write the update rule in one sentence.
- State what must always remain true.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Intuition Before Code
pages.content:
Before implementation, reason about a small example for Intervals. Ask what information can be reused and what work can safely be skipped.

- What information is repeated?
- What can be maintained incrementally?
- What changes when the input grows by one element?
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Worked Example
pages.content:
Work through a small instance of Intervals by hand. Do not code yet; write each important state transition.

- Start with the initial state.
- Apply one operation at a time.
- Record the state after every transition.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
Implement Intervals in the smallest readable version first. Separate input parsing, algorithm state, and output so debugging is localized.

- Translate the invariant into variables.
- Implement one transition at a time.
- Check the sample immediately after the first implementation.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Independent Practice
pages.content:
Now solve a fresh variation of Intervals without looking at the reference implementation. Use the same pattern but a different input arrangement or boundary.

- Restate the task.
- Choose the pattern explicitly.
- Predict the output before running.
- Test a minimum, boundary, and adversarial case.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Debugging Lab
pages.content:
Debugging Intervals should begin with the invariant and boundary conditions, not random edits.

- Check initialization.
- Check loop/condition boundaries.
- Check pointer/state movement.
- Check complexity against constraints.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

pages.title: Mastery Gate
pages.content:
You have mastered Intervals when you can explain the pattern, implement it from scratch, and transfer it to a new problem with the same underlying idea.

- Explain the invariant without code.
- Implement from a blank editor.
- Give time and space complexity.
- Name one common failure mode.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Intervals without skipping the required reasoning step.

codeExamples.title: Merge intervals
codeExamples.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){vector<pair<int,int>>a={{1,3},{2,6},{8,10}};sort(a.begin(),a.end());vector<pair<int,int>>o;for(auto x:a){if(o.empty()||x.first>o.back().second)o.push_back(x);else o.back().second=max(o.back().second,x.second);}for(auto [l,r]:o)cout<<l<<' '<<r<<"\n";}
